q-144343.name: Question 1
q-144343.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}{x}^{2}, & -2<x<2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y={X}^{2}+1,$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
q-144343.worked_solution:
First, notice that the transformation $Y={X}^{2}+1$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-2<x<2.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/8a03bd46aa6d415d8e1a49ff74557886702c1dc4bc9164ce2a5a1252874e1b4e.png)

Moreover, for $-2<x<2,$  we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $1\le y<5.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $1\le y<5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}+1\le y) \\  & =P(-(y-1)^{1/2}\le X\le (y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $1\le y<5,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})].\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[{f}_{X}((y-1)^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(-(y-1)^{1/2})] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}[\frac{3}{16}{((y-1)^{1/2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{16}{(-(y-1)^{1/2})}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(y-1)^{-1/2}(\frac{3}{16}(y-1)+\frac{3}{16}(y-1)) \\  & =\frac{3}{16}(y-1)^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{y-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{y-1}, & 1\le y<5 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Let X be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: fX(x)={316x2,−2<x<20,otherwise If Y=X2+1, then what is the probability density function of Y?

a
fY(y)={12y,0≤y<40,otherwise.
b
fY(y)={y12,1≤y<50,otherwise.
c
fY(y)={316y,0≤y<40,otherwise.
d
fY(y)={310y5,1≤y<50,otherwise.
e
fY(y)={316y−1,1≤y<50,otherwise.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that the transformation Y=X2+1 is two-to-one over the entire interval −2<x<2.

Moreover, for −2<x<2, we have that Y is nonzero on 1≤y<5.

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of Y, for 1≤y<5, we have FY(y)=P(Y≤y)=P(X2+1≤y)=P(−(y−1)1/2≤X≤(y−1)1/2)=FX((y−1)1/2)−FX(−(y−1)1/2).

To compute the PDF fY(y) for 1≤y<5, we differentiate FY with respect to y using the chain rule. This gives

fY(y)=FY′(y)=12(y−1)−1/2⋅FX′((y−1)1/2)+12(y−1)−1/2⋅FX′(−(y−1)1/2)=12(y−1)−1/2⋅fX((y−1)1/2)+12(y−1)−1/2⋅fX(−(y−1)1/2)=12(y−1)−1/2[fX((y−1)1/2)+fX(−(y−1)1/2)].

Applying the definition of fX, we finally arrive at

fY(y)=12(y−1)−1/2[fX((y−1)1/2)+fX(−(y−1)1/2)]=12(y−1)−1/2[316((y−1)1/2)2+316(−(y−1)1/2)2]=12(y−1)−1/2(316(y−1)+316(y−1))=316(y−1)1/2=316y−1.

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of Y is

fY(y)={316y−1,1≤y<50,otherwise.

q-144031.name: Question 2
q-144031.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{4}, & -1<x<3 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If $Y={(1-X)}^{2},$ then what is the probability density function of $Y?$
q-144031.worked_solution:
First, notice that the transformation $Y={(1-X)}^{2}$ is two-to-one over the entire interval $-1<x<3.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/03718360bf910c74c22b36f34ad2f63bfad6d9387c0cdc62d3fb366a52f356c9.png)

Moreover, for $-1<x<3,$ we have that $Y$ is nonzero on $0\le y<4.$ 

Now, using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0\le y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({(1-X)}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}\le 1-X\le {y}^{1/2}) \\  & =P(-{y}^{1/2}-1\le -X\le {y}^{1/2}-1) \\  & =P(1-{y}^{1/2}\le X\le 1+{y}^{1/2}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})-{F}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0\le y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\cdot {f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}({f}_{X}(1+{y}^{1/2})+{f}_{X}(1-{y}^{1/2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}(\frac{1+{y}^{1/2}}{4}+\frac{1-{y}^{1/2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the full expression for the PDF of $Y$ is

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4\sqrt{y}}, & 0\le y<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$

q-144920.name: Question 3
q-144920.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{12}(2-x), & -3<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y={X}^{2}$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<1 \\ h(y), & 1\le y<9 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $g(y).$
q-144920.worked_solution:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y={X}^{2}$ over the interval $-3<x<1.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/7332c58097d1a2933c10152028bc715a147e820ae14b2fae92fe288eaf956ce0.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $-3<x\le -1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $1\le y<9.$

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $-1<x<1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<1.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<1.$ 

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P({X}^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt{y}\le X\le \sqrt{y}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(\sqrt{y})-{F}_{X}(-\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<1,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(-\sqrt{y})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(-\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}(\frac{1}{12}(2-\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{12}(2+\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{1}{6\sqrt{y}}.$

q-144034.name: Question 4
q-144034.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}, & 0<x<5 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y=(X-3)^{2}$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<4 \\ h(y), & 4\le y<9 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $g(y).$
q-144034.worked_solution:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=(X-3)^{2}$ over the interval $0<x<5.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/6b75d7be28fd4ec38257d1a8899960f38ce616e504e02f5f371620509afe81ac.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $0<x\le 1.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $4\le y<9.$

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $1<x<5.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<4.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<4.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P((X-3)^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt{y}\le X-3\le \sqrt{y}) \\  & =P(3-\sqrt{y}\le X\le 3+\sqrt{y}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(3+\sqrt{y})-{F}_{X}(3-\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(3+\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(3-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(3+\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(3-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(3+\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(3-\sqrt{y})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(3+\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(3-\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{1}{5\sqrt{y}}.$

Question 4
?

Let X be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: fX(x)={15,0<x<50,otherwise If the probability density function of Y=(X−3)2 is given by fY(y)={g(y),0<y<4h(y),4≤y<90,otherwise find the function g(y).

a
15y3
b
15y
c
15y
d
110y
e
110y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's visualize the transformation Y=(X−3)2 over the interval 0<x<5.

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval 0<x≤1. On this interval, Y is nonzero on 4≤y<9.

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval 1<x<5. On this interval, Y is nonzero on 0<y<4.

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval 0<y<4.

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of Y, for 0<y<4, we have FY(y)=P(Y≤y)=P((X−3)2≤y)=P(−y≤X−3≤y)=P(3−y≤X≤3+y)=FX(3+y)−FX(3−y).

To compute the PDF fY(y) for 0<y<4, we differentiate FY with respect to y using the chain rule. This gives fY(y)=FY′(y)=12y⋅FX′(3+y)+12y⋅FX′(3−y)=12y⋅fX(3+y)+12y⋅fX(3−y)=12y(fX(3+y)+fX(3−y)).

Applying the definition of fX, we finally arrive at fY(y)=12y(fX(3+y)+fX(3−y))=12y(15+15)=15y.

Consequently, g(y)=15y.

q-144270.name: Question 5
q-144270.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}x, & 0<x<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<\frac{1}{2} \\ h(y), & \frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $h(y).$
q-144270.worked_solution:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ over the interval $0<x<4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/163ffe5a4c5bcbce95369f8082c8dbfababe7c40315d8136d79c9e370f05a1a1.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $0<x<2.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<\frac{1}{2}.$

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $2\le x<4.$ On this interval,  $Y$ is nonzero on  $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2}.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2}.$ 

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(\frac{1}{2}|X-1|\le y) \\  & =P(|X-1|\le 2y) \\  & =P(X-1\le 2y) \\  & =P(X\le 2y+1) \\  & ={F}_{X}(2y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we used $|X-1|=X-1$ for $X>1.$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2},$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =2{F}_{X}^{′}(2y+1) \\  & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{8}(2y+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(2y+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $h(y)=\frac{1}{4}(2y+1).$

q-144914.name: Question 6
q-144914.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{2-x}, & x\ge 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y=(X-4)^{2}$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<4 \\ h(y), & y\ge 4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $g(y).$
q-144914.worked_solution:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=(X-4)^{2}$ over the interval $x\ge 2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/77008820197d69dc81d674a48e207b7527d2f3d4cc1d0ca3ed8ad4d8553665b8.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $2<x<6.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<4.$

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $x\ge 6.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $y\ge 4.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<4.$

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P((X-4)^{2}\le y) \\  & =P(-\sqrt{y}\le X-4\le \sqrt{y}) \\  & =P(4-\sqrt{y}\le X\le 4+\sqrt{y}) \\  & ={F}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})-{F}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y}).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<4,$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(4+\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {F}_{X}^{′}(4-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\cdot {f}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y})).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({f}_{X}(4+\sqrt{y})+{f}_{X}(4-\sqrt{y})) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}({e}^{2-4-\sqrt{y}}+{e}^{2-4+\sqrt{y}}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{y}-2}+{e}^{\sqrt{y}-2}}{2\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{y}-2}+{e}^{\sqrt{y}-2}}{2\sqrt{y}}.$

Let X be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function: fX(x)={e2−x,x≥20,otherwise If the probability density function of Y=(X−4)2 is given by fY(y)={g(y),0<y<4h(y),y≥40,otherwise find the function g(y).

a
e−y−2+ey−2
b
e−y−2+ey−22y
c
e−y−2y
d
ey−22y
e
e−y+ey4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's visualize the transformation Y=(X−4)2 over the interval x≥2.

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval 2<x<6. On this interval, Y is nonzero on 0<y<4.

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval x≥6. On this interval, Y is nonzero on y≥4.

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval 0<y<4.

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of Y, for 0<y<4, we have FY(y)=P(Y≤y)=P((X−4)2≤y)=P(−y≤X−4≤y)=P(4−y≤X≤4+y)=FX(4+y)−FX(4−y).

To compute the PDF fY(y) for 0<y<4, we differentiate FY with respect to y using the chain rule. This gives fY(y)=FY′(y)=12y⋅FX′(4+y)+12y⋅FX′(4−y)=12y⋅fX(4+y)+12y⋅fX(4−y)=12y(fX(4+y)+fX(4−y)).

Applying the definition of fX, we finally arrive at fY(y)=12y(fX(4+y)+fX(4−y))=12y(e2−4−y+e2−4+y)=e−y−2+ey−22y.

Consequently, g(y)=e−y−2+ey−22y.

q-144913.problem:
Let $X$ be a continuous random variable with the following probability density function:

$$
{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{8}x, & 0<x<4 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

If the probability density function of $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ is given by 

$$
{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & 0<y<\frac{1}{2} \\ h(y), & \frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

find the function $g(y).$
q-144913.worked_solution:
First, let's visualize the transformation $Y=\frac{1}{2}|X-1|$ over the interval $0<x<4.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14231916/assets/163ffe5a4c5bcbce95369f8082c8dbfababe7c40315d8136d79c9e370f05a1a1.png)

Notice the following:

- The transformation is two-to-one over the interval $0<x<2.$ On this interval, $Y$ is nonzero on $0<y<\frac{1}{2}.$

- The transformation is one-to-one over the interval $2\le x<4.$ On this interval,  $Y$ is nonzero on  $\frac{1}{2}\le y<\frac{3}{2}.$

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval $0<y<\frac{1}{2}.$ 

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of $Y,$ for $0<y<\frac{1}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & =P(Y\le y) \\  & =P(\frac{1}{2}|X-1|\le y) \\  & =P(|X-1|\le 2y) \\  & =P(-2y\le X-1\le 2y) \\  & =P(1-2y\le X\le 2y+1) \\  & ={F}_{X}(2y+1)-{F}_{X}(1-2y).\end{aligned}
$$

To compute the PDF ${f}_{Y}(y)$ for $0<y<\frac{1}{2},$ we differentiate ${F}_{Y}$ with respect to $y$ using the chain rule. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={F}_{Y}^{′}(y) \\  & =2{F}_{X}^{′}(2y+1)+2{F}_{X}^{′}(1-2y) \\  & =2{f}_{X}(2y+1)+2{f}_{X}(1-2y) \\  & =2({f}_{X}(2y+1)+{f}_{X}(1-2y)).\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the definition of ${f}_{X},$ we finally arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & =2({f}_{X}(2y+1)+{f}_{X}(1-2y)) \\  & =2(\frac{1}{8}(2y+1)+\frac{1}{8}(1-2y)) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $g(y)=\frac{1}{2}.$

12

First, let's visualize the transformation Y=12|X−1| over the interval 0<x<4.

Notice the following:

  • The transformation is two-to-one over the interval 0<x<2. On this interval, Y is nonzero on 0<y<12.

  • The transformation is one-to-one over the interval 2≤x<4. On this interval, Y is nonzero on 12≤y<32.

In this question, we're asked to consider only the interval 0<y<12.

Using the definition of the cumulative distribution of Y, for 0<y<12, we have FY(y)=P(Y≤y)=P(12|X−1|≤y)=P(|X−1|≤2y)=P(−2y≤X−1≤2y)=P(1−2y≤X≤2y+1)=FX(2y+1)−FX(1−2y).
